name: Umar Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: This week was mostly lab: two afternoons of titrations and one of soil sampling out on the university's playing fields, mud up to my knees. I'm doing environmental science, so there's a lot of chemistry and maths I half forgot from school. I live in a flat above a kebab shop with three others, and we have a rota for the washing-up that nobody follows. On Wednesdays I play five-a-side, and on Sundays I ring my parents, who are a civil engineer and a GP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped and that people should keep their critical thinking sharp. I'd probably joke online that my stats software has had a chat assistant for years and it still can't read a messy spreadsheet. At home my dad would say the same thing about engineering software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm quite relaxed. Environmental science depends on fieldwork and judgement, so a plateau leaves my plans intact. The real worry is climate itself, and whether there'll be jobs in it that actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am: labs, field trips, the occasional AI explanation when I'm stuck on a stats idea. I'd apply for a summer placement with the county council's water team, because my dad knows someone there. I'd keep my five-a-side night and not change much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My family can pay for everything, and I have good results, so I'm in a lucky position and I know it. I just don't want to be smug about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're relaxed about this one. What would still keep you awake in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The climate jobs market, honestly. Plenty of graduates in my field end up in short contracts or consultancy. A plateau wouldn't fix that, and I'd like the government to fund proper green jobs, not just talk about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change whether you keep using AI now and then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep it as a stats tutor and nothing more. It's useful once you've checked it against a textbook, but I've caught the chatbot making a confident error in a chemistry calculation, and that's how I know to keep it on a short leash.

say: I'd say it's **overhyped** and people should keep their critical thinking sharp.
I'd joke that my stats software **still can't read** a messy spreadsheet.
think: Privately I'm **relaxed**, because fieldwork and judgement keep my plans intact.
My real worry is whether **climate jobs** will pay properly.
do: Keep up labs, field trips and the **occasional AI explanation** for stats.
Apply for a summer placement with the county council's **water team**.
feel: **Calm**, lucky in my family's backing, and trying not to be smug.
S0.quote: I've caught the chatbot making a confident error in a chemistry calculation, and that's how I know to keep it on a short leash.
fieldNote: His AI use is **narrow and checked**, which suits his steady adaptability.
Calm comes from his **family cushion**, and he names that himself.
His real worry is **green-jobs funding**, which fits his progressive outlook.

steps.text: Keep using AI only to explain stats ideas and check it against a textbook
Apply for the county council water team summer placement
Vote for parties that fund permanent green jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we should make sure it's shared fairly. In seminars I'd argue that the time saved should mean shorter working weeks, not fewer people. My housemate in computing thinks I'm naive, and we'd argue about it over pasta.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm uneasy. Data cleaning, modelling and report writing could all be taken over, and those are the jobs graduates start in. My own job in a few years might look quite different from what my lecturers describe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI more deliberately, learning to check models rather than just run them. I'd take the data science option next year, and ask my dad whether his firm hires graduates who can read both the field data and the software output. I'd also join the students' union environment society, where people argue policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like waiting for a train in fog: I know it's coming, I just can't see how fast. But I have time, which most people don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some of the thinking tasks go to AI. Which parts of environmental science do you think go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the number crunching and the first draft of any report. The bit that stays human is turning up on a muddy riverbank and deciding which sample is dodgy, and I'd want to be really good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who benefits most in that world, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies that own the biggest systems, and investors in them. I'd like to see shared ownership or a levy, so everyone gets something. If it goes the other way, people like my mum, who sees patients on low incomes every day, will pay the price.

say: I'd say the time saved should mean **shorter working weeks**, not fewer people.
I'd argue the benefits must be **shared fairly**, even if my housemate calls it naive.
think: Privately I'm **uneasy**: the data and writing tasks graduates start with could go first.
My job in a few years could look **very different** from what my lecturers describe.
do: Take the **data science option** next year and learn to check models.
Ask my dad whether his firm hires people who can read **field data** and software output.
feel: **Uneasy**, like waiting for a train in fog, but I have time.
S1.quote: The bit that stays human is turning up on a muddy riverbank and deciding which sample is dodgy, and I'd want to be really good at that.
fieldNote: He separates **desk analysis** from fieldwork judgement, a useful and concrete split.
His progressive views show up as a wish for **shared ownership** or a levy.
He feels he has **time**, which keeps him at uneasy and not anxious.

steps.text: Take the data science option next year
Practise checking model outputs against field data instead of just running them
Join the students' union environment society and argue for a levy on big AI firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to act now and that we shouldn't let a few companies decide how this goes. I'd probably sign every petition and go to a march, which I've never done. I'd tell my lecturers we need honest answers about what the degree is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. Two years is nothing: I'd be a second-year when thinking AI can do most of what I'm training for. I'd wonder if I've picked the wrong thing, and then wonder if any choice would have been right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying because there's nothing better to do, and I'd try to build skills that look more physical or local: fieldwork, lab technique, working with farmers and councils. I'd also ask my parents about savings, and whether our family has a plan. I'd push to join a working group at the students' union about what universities owe us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel safe in the short term because my parents' savings are solid, but the future part is a blank. It's a strange feeling, like being on a good boat and not knowing where the river goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is fast. What happens to the way you feel about your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mum, Dad, I don't think my degree will lead where we thought, and I'm not sure what to do instead. They'd say stay calm and keep studying, and my mum would remind me that her patients still need people in a room. I'd feel better for saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to tell your parents on the phone that night, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both, to be fair. I'd keep the degree because it teaches me to think, but I'd stop assuming a job at the end of it is guaranteed. That's a harder idea to carry around than I expected.

say: I'd say governments must act now and **not leave it** to a few companies.
I'd ask lecturers for **honest answers** about what our degree is for.
think: Privately I'd be **scared**: two years is nothing for what I'm training for.
I'd wonder if I picked the **wrong subject**, then if any choice would have been right.
do: Build **physical, local skills** like fieldwork and lab technique, working with farmers and councils.
Ask my parents about **savings** and join a students' union working group.
feel: **Anxious**, like being on a good boat without knowing where the river goes.
S2.quote: I'd keep the degree because it teaches me to think, but I'd stop assuming a job at the end of it is guaranteed.
fieldNote: The family cushion keeps him from panic but not from **real fear about direction**.
He moves toward **hands-on, local skills** as a hedge.
Telling his parents is a **relief step**, showing how much he leans on them.

steps.text: Seek out fieldwork and lab technique work with farmers and councils
Ask my parents about family savings and a plan
Join a students' union working group on what universities owe us
Sign petitions and go to a march demanding government action

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get this right if people start now, and that universities should rewrite what they teach. I'd tell friends to take it seriously but not panic, which is also what I tell myself. I'd post about it rarely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's manageable. Five years takes me through the degree and a year or two beyond, and robots arrive three years after that. My field has a lot of outdoor, practical work that would be late to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the time to build a profile that mixes data skills with real field experience. I'd do a summer placement every year, and a masters if the market looks rough. I'd also save a bit from my allowance, because a cushion is a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. I'd feel like I had a plan, which helps a lot. It's the difference between a storm warning and a storm that just arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is a different feeling from two. What do you do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes, toward something with more data, like environmental data science. But I'd do it in second year, after seeing what employers say. Rushing a change now just because of fear would be silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider switching course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I can show that I make a difference on the ground, that's my best protection. A good reference from a muddy riverbank beats a perfect CV, so I'd spend the five years being useful to a council, a farm or a charity.

say: I'd say there's **time** to get this right if people start now.
I'd tell friends to take it seriously, **but not panic**.
think: Privately I think it's **manageable**, because outdoor practical work changes late.
I feel a plan makes the difference between a **storm warning** and a surprise.
do: Do a **summer placement** every year and consider a masters if the market looks rough.
Save a little from my **allowance**, because a cushion is a cushion.
feel: **Uneasy but steady**, because having a plan helps a lot.
S3.quote: A good reference from a muddy riverbank beats a perfect CV, so I'd spend the five years being useful to a council, a farm or a charity.
fieldNote: Longer time turns his fear into **a plan** of placements and field credit.
He chooses **wait and decide** on switching to data science until second year.
He trusts **real references** more than certificates.

steps.text: Do a summer placement with a council or farm every year
Save part of my monthly allowance in a separate account
Decide about switching to environmental data science after second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough if we spend it on training and fair rules rather than arguing. I'd go on to tell my parents' generation to stop assuming younger people can fix it alone. I'd probably write a student newspaper piece about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm calm. I'd be 29 and have years of practice before robots reach practical jobs. It's the same end point, but I have time to be someone who can supervise the systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, then work in the field for a few years, then do a masters in data and environmental policy. I'd stay active in the environment society and vote for parties with serious retraining plans. I'd keep using AI sometimes, but only for things I can verify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of curiosity. If the future arrives slowly enough, I might even enjoy it. I could imagine automation making fieldwork safer and cheaper, which would be good news for the planet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years gives a lot of room. Does it feel almost too comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. People get complacent when they have ten years. I'd watch for the date creeping up and for friends saying they'll sort things later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who or what do you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies chasing short-term profit, and shareholders who want quick returns. Systems don't decide who gets the benefit, people with money do, so I'd blame shareholders chasing quick returns more than the technology.

say: I'd say ten years is enough **if we spend it** on training and fair rules.
I'd write a student newspaper piece telling older people **not to leave** it to us.
think: Privately I'm **calm**, with years of practice before robots reach practical work.
I could imagine automation making **fieldwork safer** and cheaper.
do: Finish my degree, work a few years, then do a **masters** in data and environmental policy.
Keep using AI only for things I can **verify**, and vote for retraining plans.
feel: **Calm**, with some curiosity about how it could help the planet.
S4.quote: Systems don't decide who gets the benefit, people with money do, so I'd blame shareholders chasing quick returns more than the technology.
fieldNote: Blame is aimed at **short-term profit motives**, not at technology itself.
He pictures **automation helping** environmental fieldwork, a hopeful turn.
He worries about **complacency** when time is long.

steps.text: Work a few years in the field, then do a masters in environmental data policy
Vote for parties with serious retraining plans
Use AI only for tasks I can verify myself

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, since I'd be a second-year when it lands and my field still depends on people trusting data. What would help is public money for retraining, and rules that make companies show what their systems do. I'd also like universities to say plainly what a degree is for in that world.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I use AI tools sometimes, mostly to explain a stats concept I missed. I don't let it write for me, because lab reports are marked on my own reasoning. My degree is meant to teach me how to doubt a number properly, and I can't see a machine making that skill worthless. People assume students either use it for everything or never touch it, and I'm in the middle.

headlineQuote: My degree is meant to teach me how to doubt a number properly, and I can't see a machine making that skill worthless.
portrait: Umar is 19, in his first year of **environmental science**, with a strong family cushion and top results.
He is progressive and steady: he uses AI tools **now and then** and changes habits once something is proven.
He thinks in terms of **evidence and rules**, and wants public money and company transparency.
His mood climbs with warning time, and he blames **shareholders and short-term thinking** more than the technology.
His parents, an engineer and a GP, are his sounding board, and he would act through study and voting.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most, because it lands while he is still a second-year student.
whatWouldHelp: **Public retraining money** and rules making companies show what their systems do.
Universities saying plainly **what a degree** is for in that world.
